title: DexCom, Inc., Q3 2026 Earnings Call, Oct 29, 2026

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Dexcom Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Release Conference Call. My name is Abby, and I will be your operator for today's call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, the conference is being recorded.
I will now turn the call over to Sean Christensen, Senior Vice President of Finance and Investor Relations. Sean, you may begin.

segments.speaker: Sean Christensen
paras: Thank you, operator, and welcome to DexCom's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. Our agenda begins with Jake Leach, Dexcom's President and CEO, who will summarize our recent highlights and ongoing strategic initiatives, followed by a financial review and outlook from Jereme Sylvain, our Chief Operating Officer and Chief Financial Officer. Following our prepared remarks, we will open the call up for your questions. At that time, we ask analysts to limit themselves to 1 question each so we can provide an opportunity for everyone participating today. Please note that there are also slides available related to our third quarter 2026 performance on the Dexcom Investor Relations website on the Events and Presentations page.

With that, let's review our safe harbor statement. Some statements on today's call may constitute forward-looking statements. These statements reflect management's intentions, beliefs and expectations about future events, strategies, competition, products, operating plans and performance. These statements are made as of the date hereof based on information currently available to Dexcom, are subject to various risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. For a discussion of these risks, please see DexCom's annual report on Form 10-K, most recent quarterly report on Form 10-Q and other filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Except as required by law, we assume no obligation to update any forward-looking statement or to conform any forward-looking statements to actual results.

Additionally, during the call, we will discuss certain non-GAAP financial measures. Unless otherwise noted, all financial measures discussed on this call are presented on a non-GAAP basis. Non-GAAP measures should not be considered in isolation or as a substitute for or superior to GAAP results. Please refer to the tables in our earnings release and the slides accompanying our third quarter 2026 earnings call for reconciliations to the most directly comparable GAAP measure.
Now I will turn it over to Jake.

segments.speaker: Jacob Leach
paras: Thank you, Sean, and thank you, everyone, for joining us. Today, we reported third quarter revenue growth of 11% compared to the third quarter of 2025 on both a reported and organic basis. Underlying our third quarter results are 4 key areas that advance our long-term vision we provided earlier this year. First, we continue to see strong momentum across the CGM category driving our stable low double-digit revenue growth with active base growth above those levels. We once again gained share in the quarter, supported by prescriber and customer preference for Dexcom CGM, positioning us well as we prepare for significant access expansion. .

Second, our clinical evidence continues to strengthen the case for broader access to CGM. Third, our product portfolio continues to advance, helping us deliver a more personalized and valuable experience for each customer. And fourth, our operational execution has given us upward momentum throughout the year, strengthening our scale and financial position while also driving strong product performance in the field.

In the U.S., we again delivered strong revenue growth of 14% and captured share across the market. This extended a multi-quarter trend of share gains in the U.S. with our largest increase coming from customers with type 2 diabetes, including those not on insulin. We continue to see greater physician awareness of the role Dexcom CGM can play across the spectrum of diabetes. This is contributing to growth today and preparing the market for a significantly broader coverage environment in the future. Along those lines, we continue to expect CMS to announce a type 2 non-insulin coverage decision this year as the case for reimbursement is strengthening. Much of this confidence is driven by Connect, our Type 2 randomized controlled trial, which is now widely recognized as the landmark CGM study for this population.

As a reminder, we announced the results of Connect this summer at the 2026 ADA scientific sessions and could not have been happier with the results. Over a 6-month study period, we saw a 1.6% A1c improvement for the Dexcom CGM Group, which equated to a 0.9% difference in A1c between the CGM arm and the control group. These are the strongest A1c results we have generated across our historic randomized controlled trials, which have helped shape standards of care and establish broad reimbursement. We now expect Connect to do the same thing for the type 2 non-insulin population.

Earlier this month, Connect was published in the New England Journal of Medicine. This provides an important level of independent validation and give the study a prominent platform among clinicians, advocacy organizations and reimbursement bodies around the world. This marks the first time in nearly 2 decades that the New England Journal of Medicine published clinical data on the stand-alone use of CGM. While we believe our results speak for themselves, this publication reinforces both the quality of the data and its potential to reshape clinical practice.

As a next step towards broader coverage, we provided this publication update directly to the medical directors evaluating the submission for Medicare coverage expansion. We also look forward to seeing this evidence included in upcoming clinical standards, including the ADA standards of care, which is expected to be updated in the coming weeks. Connect further strengthens the growing body of evidence supporting the broader benefit of CGM across metabolic health. This includes significant improvements across multiple studies in 10-year cardiovascular disease risk, blood pressure, cholesterol, triglycerides and kidney disease progression. Our expanding clinical evidence is supported by a product portfolio designed around the distinct needs of each customer.

During the third quarter, we launched a fully redesigned Stelo app. The new Stelo app experience is more intuitive and personalized with enhanced glucose insights, simplified meal logging and more detailed nutritional information. This is especially important because many Stelo customers are engaging with their glucose data for the first time, helping them understand how food and lifestyle choices affect their glucose can make the information more useful and actionable. Just as importantly, the redesigned app establishes a new software foundation for which our broader product experience can evolve.

Stelo gives us a platform to introduce new capabilities, learn from customer engagement and ultimately bring the most valuable innovations across our broader product portfolio. This supports the goal we outlined at Investor Day to deliver greater personalization and engagement across every stage of the customer journey. During the quarter, we also continued to advance the rollout of our G7 15-day system with broad pump connectivity available as of this summer, customer adoption steadily built throughout the quarter. This leaves us on track to convert nearly 50% of our U.S. customer base, the G7 15-day by year-end. Importantly, feedback from physicians and customers continues to be positive, particularly around the extended wear time, sensor performance and updated patch design. In fact, as the updated adhesive is rolling out into the field, we've already seen a 4- to 5-point improvement in 15 days survivability. We are now preparing to bring these benefits to customers outside the United States.

Earlier this year, Health Canada became the first international regulator to clear G7 15-day. Beginning in November, we will officially launch this product in Canada, marking the first of several planned international introductions in the coming quarters. We also received clearance in the third quarter in Japan, positioning us for a launch in that market in early 2027. I'm encouraged by the level of execution we've delivered in 2026, including the third quarter. During the quarter, we delivered further manufacturing efficiencies, improved freight costs and saw strong product performance in the field. We also reached an important milestone at our Ireland facility, which recently initiated commercial production on schedule. Ireland expands our manufacturing capacity and strengthens the resilience of our global supply network.

With large-scale manufacturing plants now in the U.S., Europe and Asia Pacific, we have the capacity to support our ambitious growth plans ahead. We are also expanding our digital customer support ecosystem into select international markets, including My Dexcom account. Building on the strong adoption we've seen in the U.S., these tools help simplify the support experience improve efficiency and save time for our customers. This is another example of our commitment to setting the standard for customer experience. This continued progress reflects our team's focus and discipline throughout the year. Across the business, we have advanced several important strategic initiatives while continuing to deliver strong growth, margin and cash flow generation.

As we look toward DexCom's next chapter, it is critical that we have the right leadership and operating structure to scale with that same discipline. In line with that goal, we recently promoted Jereme Sylvain to Chief Operating Officer in addition to his responsibilities as Chief Financial Officer. Jeremy is an exceptional leader and trusted partner with a deep understanding of every part of our business, expanding his role to include operations, quality and customer success, brings these functions even closer to our financial and strategic priorities as we work to reach millions more people around the world.
With that, I will turn it over to Jereme.

segments.speaker: Jereme Sylvain
paras: Thank you, Jake. As a reminder, unless otherwise noted, the financial metrics presented today will be discussed on a non-GAAP basis. Reconciliations to GAAP can be found in today's earnings release as well as the slide deck on our IR website. .

For the third quarter of 2026, we reported worldwide revenue of $1.34 billion compared to $1.21 billion for the third quarter of 2025, representing growth of 11% on both a reported basis and organic basis. As a reminder, our definition of organic revenue excludes the impact of foreign exchange in addition to non-CGM revenue acquired or divested in the trailing 12 months. U.S. revenue totaled $970 million for the third quarter compared to $852 million in the third quarter of 2025, representing an increase of 14%. As Jake mentioned, we again took share in the U.S. market with strong performance across all customer segments. This helped drive a nice acceleration in our U.S. growth rate compared to the first half of the year. global new patient starts were near record levels in Q3, consistent with our expectation as seasonality continues to evolve in the business.

Relative to the prior year, New customer starts were up in the third quarter with these efforts amplified by our focused efforts on retention and utilization to maximize our growth algorithm. International revenue grew 5% on both on a reported and organic basis. totaling $375 million in the third quarter. As we've discussed in previous quarters, the second half of 2025 saw multiple reimbursement wins that we are lapping as we move through the third and fourth quarters of 2026. We've seen a similar dynamic in prior years as the timing of these reimbursement decisions can create some quarterly variability in international growth rates. As usual, we expect this to be a short-term dynamic with international revenue normalizing back to higher organic growth levels at the start of next year.

We are very excited about the business based on the number of drivers on the horizon, including new access wins, the rollout of G7 15-day, Dexcom 1+ 15-day, Stelo, a full year of Dexcom Flex and continued GoDirect opportunities. We have not seen significant changes to our pricing environment, and we are executing the access expansion and go-to-market strategy that we discussed at Investor Day.

Our third quarter gross profit was $875.3 million or 65.1% of revenue compared to 61.3% of revenue in the third quarter of 2025. we delivered another quarter of strong gross margin performance, with margins up approximately 380 basis points compared to last year. This reflected continued manufacturing efficiencies further progress in freight and quality management and a benefit from the continued ramp-up of G7 15-day in the U.S. market. Operating expenses were $535.8 million for Q3 of 2026, compared to $468.4 million in Q3 of 2025. Operating income was $339.5 million or 25.3% of revenue in the third quarter of 2026, compared to $272.9 million or 22.6% of revenue in the same quarter of 2025.

We again delivered solid operating margin expansion during the quarter despite increased investment in Ireland as we prepare that facility for commercial production. Excluding the Ireland facility, we would have again delivered OpEx leverage in the quarter. Adjusted EBITDA was $435.2 million or 32.4% of revenue for the third quarter compared to $368.4 million or 30.5% of revenue for the third quarter of 2025. Net income for the third quarter was $275 million or $0.73 per share.

We remain in a great financial position, closing the quarter with approximately $1.8 billion of cash and cash equivalents. Our cash flow generation continues to stand out as we have now generated over $900 million of free cash flow through the first 3 quarters of the year. This enabled us to already execute our Investor Day goal of repurchasing $1 billion of stock in 2026. Having completed that, we are announcing another $1 billion share repurchase authorization in line with our commitment to deploy at least 50% of free cash flow generated over the course of 2027.

During Investor Day, we also spoke to our broader framework for assessing tuck-in M&A. Historically, acquiring international distributors has been 1 of our highest value uses of capital and a key part of our strategy to transition to direct operations in select markets. Today, we are announcing another international distribution deal. We recently signed a deal to acquire a business from a partner that allows us to go direct across high potential markets in Europe. As we shared at Investor Day, these decisions to go direct to help ensure that we have control and alignment as we significantly expand access to CGM in key markets.

Turning to guidance. We are updating our revenue guidance to be in the range of $5.20 billion to $5.25 billion, representing growth of 12% to 13% for the year. At the midpoint, our updated outlook passes through the third quarter revenue outperformance partially offset by approximately $5 million of incremental foreign exchange headwinds since last quarter. This also implies midpoint fourth quarter growth of 10%. For margins, we are maintaining our full year non-GAAP gross profit margin guidance at approximately 64%. We are increasing our non-GAAP operating profit margin guidance to approximately 24% and adjusted EBITDA margin guidance to approximately 32%.
With that, we can open up the call for Q&A. Sean?

segments.speaker: Sean Christensen
paras: Thank you, Jereme. As a reminder, we ask our audience to limit themselves to only 1 question at this time and then reenter the queue if necessary. Operator, please provide the Q&A instructions. .

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: [Operator Instructions] And our first question comes from the line of Matt Taylor with Jefferies.

segments.speaker: Matthew Taylor
paras: Congrats on the nice results. I thought maybe I'd start at a high level and I wanted you to address the debate around category growth. We saw your competitor call out some pricing headwinds that you just said in the prepared remarks, you're not really seeing that. So maybe you could comment on that specifically and what you think about overall category growth today before we're getting this CMS announcement. .

segments.speaker: Jacob Leach
paras: Yes. Thanks, Matt, for the question. And I really appreciate the opportunity to be able to give you guys our perspective on this because there has been, as you mentioned, some recent noise out there about the category. I think if you look at the way that this year has played out, from our perspective, nothing has changed in our view of the opportunity in front of us. we put out our LRP at our Investor Day this summer, and we are still extremely confident in that plan that we put forward. As you look at the way we guided for this year, we looked at the current coverage environment, and we specifically mentioned that we didn't anticipate any expansions in coverage this year, at least that's how we based our plan -- and we basically guided to a range of new customer starts with the bottom of our growth range and that strong customer starts, but not record. .

And then the top end of our guide was -- would reflect a record year of new patient starts. As you've seen, we've continually raised our guidance, and we're now guiding to the upper range of our original guidance we issued in January. And that's because we're tracking to a record new patient year. And so as you look at that against the backdrop of current coverage, we feel very confident in our ability to grow in this environment. Our active base growth is in the upper teens, and you can see the revenue growth. And so we're confident in our ability to grow in this category.

segments.speaker: Jereme Sylvain
paras: Yes, to your question, Matt, on pricing, I think you asked a question on pricing and can you talk to that? I think it's pretty clear. We haven't seen a degradation of pricing around the world. Certainly, as we move outside the U.S. into markets that are new for us, we have a product portfolio that we go in. I think we've matched the product portfolio to the reimbursement. And I think you've seen that be relatively stable. And so I think we haven't seen some of the references that June referenced with some pricing concerns. Certainly not in the markets we've entered into in the markets we've been in -- and I think you'll see that ultimately reflected in our gross margins as our gross margins are the highest they've been since Q4 of 2022.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: Our next question comes from the line of Robbie Marcus with JPMorgan.

segments.speaker: Robert Marcus
paras: Great. question. One, I wanted to talk or ask about competition outside the U.S. Your competitors spoke to seeing pretty sharp pricing, mostly in cash pay I know U&M overlap, but not exactly some markets that are more exposed to than you. So what are you seeing outside the U.S.? How do you feel about volume growth right now? And anything new on the competitive front? Appreciate it.

segments.speaker: Jereme Sylvain
paras: Yes, certainly, I can take that. Certainly, as we think about markets outside the U.S. and monitoring pricing, it's been stable. And what I mean when we look at Certainly, when it comes to reimbursement, and we'll start with reimbursement because typically, that's how we've approached markets to begin with. We've seen the reimbursement is stable and it's usually tiered based on the acuity of the condition. And so we've seen that play out. It's why we have a product portfolio to match it and to match what the need ultimately is. And again, it's been stable. We don't exactly overlap in all fairness to your point, there's a lot of markets, I would say that maybe we don't overlap in where a competitor might be and we may not. And so ultimately, if there's a degradation in the existing business for that particular incumbent, there could be some impact there.

For example, if you were the only CGM offering in a country and someone came in there is a risk that the incumbent may have been overpriced into that window and actually with natural pressure, you come back to more market conditions. But what I would say is as we look at our portfolio and our offerings across the world, and the market conditions that exist there from all competitors in that market, I think we're priced right. And so we haven't necessarily seen that degradation at least in our book of business, and competition, I think we compete well in those markets. Clearly, the tiered portfolio was done to compete with the right patient with the right product. And when we get into these markets and we compete with that right product in that market, you can see we're taking share in those markets.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And our next question comes from the line of Travis Steed with Bank of America.

segments.speaker: Travis Steed
paras: This is Travis, sorry. I guess I wanted to ask about there was a CDS contract lost recently. I know you don't talk about payers too much, but maybe if you just talk about the potential when you do have contract losses that you're able to offset with revenue per patient and how you think about your ability to still be confident in 10% plus revenue growth in '27?

segments.speaker: Jacob Leach
paras: Travis, thank you. Yes. I think what I'll start is just talk a little bit about the landscape, particularly in the U.S., as you mentioned, payers and PBMs. And then I'll cover that. I'll cover kind of how we view it, how we think things are moving forward, and then we'll also cover what we think the impact looks like for next year. So if you look at the general access landscape, in the United States. You've got -- for CGM, you got formulary access through the pharmacy and then you've also got medical benefit access. And so specifically on the formulary side, there's a lot of custom formularies, the specific contract you're talking about is a very -- it's a particular portion of a particular PBM access.

And so when we look at PBM formularies across the United States, we're generally in an equal access position, copeverd with competitors. There are some where we're advantaged and there are some where our competitors are advantaged. But one thing I want to be clear on is as we negotiate these contracts, we are always negotiating for equal access. We feel that, that is the right thing for patients. It's the right thing for prescribers. Ultimately, I think it's the right thing for employers and the plans that service them. And we think we're very confident in our position to be able to compete in that type of a scenario. And so we're always pushing for equal access.

And I think when these types of decisions are made, one of the things that I think is important to consider is sometimes it may be suggested that the products are comparable. But I'll give you an example. Imagine there's a child out there with type 1 diabetes has been using Dexcom for 4 or 5 years. powering an AID system, getting fantastic results driven by the accuracy of our sensor, their ability to calibrate that sensor when they want to. And then the parent's ability to see their data through the share follow system anytime they want. Now if you see if that individual try to switch to a competitor, it is not compatible with their insulin pump. There's multiple pumps out there that competitors are not compatible with here in the United States. They also lose the ability to use the share follow system in collaboration.

So I think trying to consider that as a comparable product is not even in the realm of reality. The other example idea is if you have a prescriber who's prescribing Dexcom G7 to a basal insulin user because of the smart basal feature and the ability to hit those outcomes that both the patients and the prescribers will run, that's not a feature that's offered by our competitor. So I think in the realm of maybe for certain patients, those products are considered comparable, but for the vast majority, they are not. And so the good news, though, is that for patients who have potentially lost coverage through a formulary through a pharmacy. Most of them still have access through a medical benefit, and so they can still access the product through a DME.

And actually, one thing I wanted to mention is that we have a plan to launch a new system called Dexcom Direct. It is a service for patients that we've been building actually with the anticipation of the expansion into Medicare. So our plan was a Medicare coverage expanded. We wanted to be able to help those folks navigate their coverage, whether it's through a Medicare Advantage plan or through a medical benefit for fee-for-service, durable medical equipment benefit. And so that system was being developed very similar to some of the other direct services that you see out there in the marketplace. And it's all about helping our patients get access to our technology.

Again, we're originally planning to launch that in front of the Medicare expansion. But with that capability launching early next year, it is a perfect place where patients anyone, not just this example, but anyone who's having a challenge getting access to our technology can go the Dexcom Direct and we'll walk them through every step of the way to ensure that they get access to the technology they need.
Jereme, do you want to talk a little bit about how we see it moving forward?

segments.speaker: Jereme Sylvain
paras: Yes. And thanks for the question, Travis. Yes, maybe I'll give you guys some context to at least how we see it in the context of next year. And while we're not going to give guidance next year. I do think it helps give you confidence around LRP starting point for next year. So the PBM we're talking about represents less than 4% of our U.S. revenue results. So relatively small in the context of our overall company. And typically, when you think about an arrangement where you have exclusivity or preferred 1 of 1, even though it says 1/1, you typically don't get all of it. You might get 2/3 of customers and 1/3 go through various pathways, whether it's off-formulary other opportunities. .

Obviously, when you have that preferred status, there's differences in price tiers that you could probably imagine. And that's the way you typically negotiate these things. If you move off of preferred into the secondary, it typically comes with a pretty significant price increase. And so the expectation is while we navigate through this from a financial perspective, we'll talk about the patient perspective here in a second. The expectation is that it doesn't necessarily have that much of an impact on our next year results from a financial perspective. because we do expect to -- even though there might be a flip in terms of patients, the reality is, as we expect, obviously, the remuneration to change as a result of that. That's the financial piece of it. I think it's important to understand, it's important context to size it.

The underlying reality though, and Jake alluded to it is we don't like being in these situations for our patients. And so that's one of the things, the reason why Jake alluded to Dexcom Direct and working really hard to make sure there's a limited patient disruption because at the end of the day, what we want to do is come back to our mission, which is empower people they control their health. It means having access to product, making sure we don't disrupt their daily life. So we're going to work hard to make sure we keep every single patient, undisrupted as much as possible through this process. It's against the backdrop, but we don't expect to have much of a significant impact on our next year financial results.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And our next question comes from the line of Larry Biegelsen with Wells Fargo.

segments.speaker: Unknown Analyst
paras: It's Lei calling in for Larry. You mentioned some impact from the from the PBM change being modest. Can you talk about any other top line, bottom line puts and takes for '27? The consensus revenue number out there is roughly 11% growth, that's near the floor that you laid out. How should we think about U.S. growth just given kind of the coverage expectations?

segments.speaker: Jereme Sylvain
paras: Yes. So the -- we'll go back to kind of what we talked about at Investor Day in terms of how to think about it. We'll give guidance at the right time. But -- in terms of how we've talked about exiting 2026, obviously, we've made some really nice progress over the course of the year on gross margin. We're going to turn on Ireland here in the fourth quarter. So I expect there to be a little bit of an impact of Ireland ramping up into the first part of next year. But at the end of the day, underneath it all, you're still going to see more and more progression of a move to 15-day product. here, certainly in the U.S. talked about launching it in Canada. And we have a couple of other markets that are going to be launching here 15-day relatively soon. So you should start to see some of those tailwinds starting to play through next year. And then obviously, we won't have the start-up costs associated with Ireland. So those are some pretty some interesting puts and takes as we move into next year.

We'll go ahead and give the guide for next year officially as we get to that point. But I think hopefully, that gives you some puts and takes, at least to think about it that we've historically talked about -- and then, of course, we'll give you more as the right time comes.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And our next question comes from the line of Jeff Johnson with Baird.

segments.speaker: Jeffrey Johnson
paras: Maybe if I could just ask a follow-up question on the CVS question that was already asked. But Jeremy, as you explained some of those patients who might no longer have preferred access might be willing to pay the higher price to come off that preferred. Typically, what would that price increase look like? If I'm a patient who no longer has preferred access, what would I be paying per month as an increase to stay on Dexcom, number one?

And number two, I know you're working with a group to try to move some of these patients, as you talked about from pharmacy to Medical. Can you just help us understand the mechanics of that? If I'm a Dexcom G7 where can I just call that group that you're working with and say, "Hey, move me to my medical, -- do I even know as a patient what that means? And typically, what is my DME co-pay relative to my pharmacy co-pay?

segments.speaker: Jereme Sylvain
paras: Sure. Thanks, Jeff. I can take you through -- while we won't get into specific pricing because there's obviously some competitive reasons behind that. It would typically be pretty sizably higher. And the reason is, is obviously exclusive is very different than nonpreferred. And that's always embedded in contracts. And so it goes up by a pretty significant amount. In terms -- so that at least gives you some context. It's not like a 5% increase. It's much, much, much higher than that. .

In terms of then what do I do? How do I navigate through this? What we're going to do is typically what you would have to do is you have to have the script. And so you write the script, and the script would go to either the DME or the pharmacy. In this case, you'd write the script to the DME provider and the DME provider then go ahead and check in intramedia benefit to prior authorization as needed and/or if you want to go through the prior authorization route with the actual PBM, which you also have that opportunity as well, that would go through. This is where Jake referred to Dexcom Direct comes directly into play there. That's where you can send a script there. We'll do the work for you.

And so it makes it much easier for folks to understand, okay, where do I have access what are my opportunities? Can I -- can you canvass the landscape for -- do I want to go cash pay? Do I want to go do I want to try for a prior authorization. Again, we'll do that work for you. So hopefully, that makes it much easier for the patient. I think it's a good opportunity for us to make sure that we're doing that work for them. The co-pay, it varies. It really depends on your individual insurance. And so what's happened typically is the DME will have a contract with the payer in this case, the medical benefit payer. Sometimes it a percentage of the total test price. Sometimes it's a flat rate. It really depends. Typically, it's -- we typically see it in that 10% to 20% of total pay range per month. In high deductible health plans, you have the upfront cost, but then you get to full coverage going forward.

So we've kind of talked about this historically as we head a DME business. It depends on the individual payer contracts. But obviously, we'll work best using that Dexcom direct portal to try to maximize the opportunity for the individual. Hope that helps you.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And our next question comes from the line of Matthew O'Brien with Piper Sandler.

segments.speaker: Anna Runci
paras: This is Anna on for Matt. Just wanted to ask on the Connect data, now that that's fully out. Wondering how much of a contributor and type 2 patients who were to the U.S. new patient start number in the quarter. I know it's still pretty early days, but just given that commercial coverage still exists for a pretty sizable chunk of the market, -- are there any signs that Connect is starting to shift that mix? And to the extent possible, is there how much of the improvement in the quarter reflects the growth of the category versus share gains?

segments.speaker: Jacob Leach
paras: Yes. Thanks, Anna. So when we think about Connect, we're very excited to see it published in such a prominent journal, which really changes the conversation out there and it makes the data very accessible to a large population of physicians and clinicians who read that journal. And so what I'd say is it's additional evidence. We already had a pretty significant amount of evidence, but this now being kind of the landmark irrefutable evidence of how Dexcom CGM can drive improvements in this population. It's really around helping our team that's out in the field raise awareness to the fact that we have these outcomes. And so it's really changing the conversation out there more towards very broad coverage expansion as we prepare for that.

When you think about new patients to your question, the -- we are seeing a good number of non-insulin users in our new patient numbers. The insulin users are still the largest group, but the noninsulin users are not too far behind when you look at new patient numbers per quarter. And so as we continue to see coverage awareness of the coverage, I think that's been what we've been working on is making sure people are aware of that coverage because it wasn't very long ago that we got that commercial coverage for non-insulin users. And we're basically priming the pump for when the Medicare expansion occurs in that way, it will be much easier for prescribers because you get to the point where when Medicare moves, then you'll see some more of the commercial plans move, and we get to the plant were anybody who has diabetes should have access to CGM because of the benefits that we can provide across that broad spectrum of patients. So the Connect data is extremely helpful in carrying that message to all those prescribers.

segments.speaker: Jereme Sylvain
paras: And then to your question on the overall market, you kind of look at the overall market, it is -- it remains stable. I think I think you've got 2 of the 3 largest CGM players out there, and you've got -- you combine the 2 and you're still in the low double digits, specifically in the U.S. in terms of revenue growth. And so it's still a stable market. Obviously, if you look at the results, you can see -- and you can see it in various other forms. I think we're doing a nice job taking share. And so a good chunk of that is us taking share there. But it is a stable market. I think we're excited to see it continue. .

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And our next question comes from the line of Joanne Wuensch with Citi.

segments.speaker: Joanne Wuensch
paras: Did you update on the timing of expectations for non-intensive type 2 either the proposal and/or the implementation? And can you please update us on the time line or expectations for GA?

segments.speaker: Jacob Leach
paras: Thanks, Joanne. We haven't changed our perspective on the Medicare timing. We still anticipate hearing back from Medicare around the coverage decision this year. And then our current plan has that coverage taking effect the middle of next year. So nothing has changed there, very consistent. And it's consistent with the conversations we've been having. I've been spending quite a bit of time in Washington, talking to lots of different stakeholders. We've got our advocacy groups, lots of discussions going on around this coverage.

And as I mentioned in my prepared remarks, we made sure that the Medicare directors were making this decision had access to the Connect data. It was actually funny. they were very aware of the data even before it was published in the New England Journal, which I think is helpful, but we did make sure they have the official notice of that. And so yes, nothing has changed on that front at all.

And then on GA, the teams are continuing to make fantastic progress on technology. We're seeing amazing results in the clinical studies that we're running around the accuracy and performance of that platform. It's a whole new platform for us with the new electronics new sensor, everything kind of built into a 50% smaller volume with more capability than we have on the G7 platform. So making fantastic progress on that. And so nothing has changed in that timing either. We're still targeting -- depending on regulatory review time lines, either launching at the end of next year or early '28 kind of dependent on those time lines, but everything is very much on track.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And our next question comes from the line of Jayson Bedford with Raymond James.

segments.speaker: Jayson Bedford
paras: Congrats on the progress. I wanted to ask about the distributor deal that you announced and see if we can get a bit more detail. What percent of the international -- your international business is covered by this distributor? And was there any impact in 3Q or an anticipated impact in 4Q?

segments.speaker: Jereme Sylvain
paras: Yes. So it's a good question. We'll have more specific details on it as we come up. We've signed the deal, it has not closed yet. So it's not going to impact this year. It's going to close next year, Jason. So I think -- so in short, no impact in Q3, no impact in Q4. It certainly is a growth lever as we move into next year as we lean into that market. It is essentially our largest remaining distributor market in Europe. So we'll be doing some work about taking that direct. So very excited about that opportunity. here soon. But we are in the kind of sign to close phase. So in the closet make a little while just because there's a lot of conditions that heavy have to go ahead and address.

So thanks for the question. Probably have a little bit more about it as we get closer. And certainly, as we close the deal, we'll kind of give you a feel for what that size looks like, what the impact looks like. Ultimately, we'd expect as you might expect, as we take these distributors direct as a growth lever, we are willing to invest in our business in a way that obviously others may not be.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And our next question comes from the line of Steve Lichtman with William Blair.

segments.speaker: Steven Lichtman
paras: Jake, you mentioned the upcoming ADA standards of care update. Where do you hope that lands now with Connect in hand and published? And do the potential changes there give you more confidence in the ultimate coverage decision by CMS?

segments.speaker: Jacob Leach
paras: Yes. Thanks, Steve. Yes, we anticipate that the Connect data is going to influence those -- the standards of care. And what it really is, it's all about the level of evidence. So when you -- the CONNECT study is Level A evidence. And so when you have Level A evidence, it is a strong recommendation for use of the technology in that population. So we very much believe that, that will have a significant impact on the standards of care, basically making the CGM standard of care for anybody with diabetes that we're rounding out the broad in IT group. So everything from type 1 through the different stages of type 2, CGM have a significant benefit. So we do anticipate that.

And when it comes to confidence, yes, as standards of care change around the world, coverage also changes. And so as some payer systems recognize it sooner than others, but I think the important thing that we do is just keep the volume up on the noise around the benefits and make sure that everyone is aware of this new evidence that we've generated. And we're going to continue to generate evidence. We're not done here. I mean, we basically -- this is in IT, but as we look to the future, there's still lots of opportunity. If you think about the prediabetes population being able to screen that population and help them either prevent diabetes, reverse their pre-diabetes or significantly slow that progression of diabetes and all of the complications that I mentioned that come along with that. So we're very, very excited about that publication and it being out, our ability to talk about it and do feel like it's going to change standards of care around the world.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And our next question comes from the line of Bill Plovanic with Canaccord Genuity.

segments.speaker: William Plovanic
paras: Yes. It's really minus around G7 15-day and the exit rate in 2026, I think is your commentary changing? I think you said nearly 50%. You thought 50% in the past. I know it's a nuance. And then just secondly, how much will Ireland impact this year? I mean, based on the guidance, it's like 130 to 150 bps sequentially. Is that how we should be thinking it and then it gets better as you get into Q1 and Q2 of next year as you're absorbing that overhead?

segments.speaker: Jereme Sylvain
paras: Yes. So I think the 50% has always been nearly 50%. And so when we kind of gave a read coming into the year, I think the question was, where are you going to get to half? And I think we said nearly 50%. And by the way, it's tracking great towards that. So we're continuing to make good progress. And again, when we say nearly 50%, again, you're kind of making an estimation 12 months from now. And I got to say, we're pretty darn close. So certainly happy to see that, and that's been pretty consistent. And so that will be the thoughts there.

In terms of the jump-off point into next year, look, you can see some of the underlying improvement in 15-day, obviously, over the course of this year. But a lot of that ultimately is also the work we've done around working on scrap and freight and some of the challenges that we had in the prior year, and you guys are paying close attention to it. You've seen our inventory levels stabilize on our books. And I think that's really important. That's allowed us to be more efficient as we've navigated through kind of how we're going to get product around the world. So all of that has contributed. What I think is great as you can see what happens in our gross margin with the existing facilities that we have. And so that's great. It's a starting point.

Now obviously, we're guiding to a bit of a step back here in the fourth quarter. that's just going to be some of the turn on of Ireland and as we took a step back, it usually takes a few quarters for a facility to get up to kind of a normal volume ramp where you start to get back to normal. So we'll have some of those -- that drag into the first and to a lesser extent, the second and third quarter. So remember, these variances, they do amortize. And so even as you're getting more and more efficient, it does take time for when you make it when you ultimately then distribute into the system.

So I would expect us to take a little step back from -- I don't know, obviously in the fourth quarter as we move into next year. But underneath it all, I think the most important part of this is you can see where our exit rate is prior to Ireland. And obviously, as Ireland gets up to speed where our opportunity is, and that's prior to having 15 day as a majority of our product. Obviously, if we're getting to nearly 50% in the U.S. exiting this year, next year, we would expect a majority of our product, obviously, to be on G7 15-day. So I think there's some real opportunities here. We laid out some of kind of the progression drivers at Investor Day. Those are absolutely intact. And so I think that continued progression, I'd expect to see into next year, give you a little bit more color when we give official guidance, but I'd expect us to continue to make progress into next year's gross margin.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And our next question comes from the line of Mike Kratky with Leerink Partners.

segments.speaker: Michael Kratky
paras: You mentioned your focus on utility and retention metrics. So to what extent are you seeing those having a detectable impact in terms of your U.S. growth in 3Q? And can you help frame that magnitude? .

segments.speaker: Jereme Sylvain
paras: Yes. Thanks, Mike. One of the things we've been really, really focused on, and I encourage you to -- as you pay attention to all the work we're doing around customer success and the work we're doing around obviously, the product and doing all we can around enhancing the product experience. What we would -- what we're seeing is a very stable retention and utilization, and that's across a base that's growing more and more in the type 2 and IT space. .

And so I think that's a positive thing. And so we are doing some of that work. While we don't necessarily break out this is the bps from this, and this is the bips from that, I think what's important is the question often comes up, well, do you expect your retention and utilization to wane over time, especially as more and more folks come into the category. And I think the answer is, it's holding steady based on all the work we're doing around it. I think that's just an important thing to hold in the back of your mind.

We're moving to more and more folks. Those folks, I think, are seeing the value where there's an opportunity to improve the customer experience, we're absolutely taking advantage of it, and we're not done. There's a lot of things we're going to roll out here in the fourth quarter and into next year that we're really excited about. Something that we launched in the third quarter we talked about my Dexcom account and a new platform that we rolled out in the U.S. in the past. Well, that rolled out in Europe already at this point, it is rolling out in APAC shortly after that. that really starts to enhance that customer experience so that someone once they get on the product, if they do have an issue, how do we help them? How do we help them in an efficient manner? How do we make sure we meet their needs.

And then what we hope to do is how do we make it an excellent experience. where they continue to come back and they see it as a differentiator. We're going to continue to work on that. So more to come on all the initiatives, and you'll start to see them coming up time after time. But I think the most important part is those concerns that folks may have had around retention utilization as we expand deeper into the population. I think the work we're doing is holding those steady, which is a great thing.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And our next question comes from the line of Daniel Markowitz with Evercore ISI.

segments.speaker: Daniel Markowitz
paras: I wanted to talk a little bit about the basal opportunity. you talk about where we are in terms of contribution from Smart Basal? And if we could really see that step up? And if so, when?

segments.speaker: Jacob Leach
paras: Yes. Thanks, Daniel. Yes, the Smart basal technology, we've been continuing to expand our pilot launch of that technology. And we're seeing really good results, both when it comes to patient and prescriber satisfaction with the system as well as the outcomes it's driving. What we're seeing is most of these patients are getting to their optimum basal dose in about 3 weeks. -- and that's with no hypoglycemia, which is 1 of the things that folks could be challenged with if they don't have a system like this. So it's getting rapidly getting folks to their optimum dose driving the outcomes.

The thing that prescribers love about it is the patients are actually taking their insulin and they're seeing the A1c levels come down. And so we continue to broaden the pilot there. One of the things we've learned is -- and we made a bunch of adoptions to the system around the workflow. So one of the things that we knew was that we designed the system for both patients and prescribers and the different user interfaces. And what we've learned over time is that based on some of the variability we see in the different setup of the clinics, we've needed to make changes in the way of counts, the way we make connections.

The other thing, too, is that many of these prescribers want to see this capability in the EHR. So we've been using all this time to basically optimize the system to be able to roll it out even more broadly. One of the things we're working on to is right now, the system is compatible with the most popular basal insulin glargine that's out there. But we're also now working to expand its -- the algorithms capability to do [indiscernible] some of the higher consultation insulins. And so what we've learned is that to really make this an impactful feature. We want to have more compatibility with insulins. I feel that this is a very strong capability that's going to help drive our share in basal even higher because when a prescriber is thinking about basal insulin for a patient, this is the type of system you can put them on and ensure that they're going to get to that dose and ensure that they get the outcomes they're looking for in an easy and efficient way.

And the -- because the patients love it so much, they're going to take their insulin. They're going to hit that outcome. So it has an opportunity to really expand the share that we are taking in that basal market. We'll -- more to come on exactly when we're going to roll it out more broadly. But we do ultimately intend to launch it, of course, here in the U.S. broadly as well as internationally because there are basal users all over the world that could benefit from those technologies.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: Our next question comes from the line of Kieran Ryan with Deutsche Bank.

segments.speaker: Kieran Ryan
paras: Just kind of ties into the last question I wanted to ask kind of about a PCP prescriber growth and productivity. Maybe you could talk a little bit about kind of how that's trending, where you're at on the sales force coverage penetration of that broader type 2 PCP market? And then kind of within that, anything you're learning on the non-insulin side as far as turning that coverage into starts ahead of Medicare, which I know is what really moves the needle there.

segments.speaker: Jereme Sylvain
paras: Yes. Thanks for the question. This is Jereme. What we've seen in that space and we -- and maybe I'll start with the sales force and then kind of the learnings that are coming out of it. In terms of the sales force, we made the decision to expand the sales force a few years ago. It was with basal but ultimately with NIT in mind. And so we did that work and what we found over the years is there might be groups in areas that pop up and we might slightly modify sizes of territories because new prescribers are popping up and -- so I think we're doing a nice job tweaking it without making massive changes to the sales force. So that's the first started. I think we have a pretty stable sales force. I would say, a stable and efficient sales force which is great, and we're seeing great results from that team.

One of the things that we've learned is we've learned that, one, it's important to find the right prescribers that have the right patient group, obviously, if it's an NIT group with all Medicare patients. ahead of Medicare expansion. It doesn't make sense to go and push noninsulin there. And so it's one of those things where as we learn more and more about the prescribers and ultimately, how they're prescribing, what they're prescribing. I think the team is getting ever more efficient about making sure they customize the approach they get to the physician's office. Because you know this, I know this. We've all talked about this. You only get so much time with a physician in a primary care office. They're very, very busy. They're seeing patients all day long. And so it's making sure we're maximizing those touch points wherever we can.

And we're using all sorts of tools to do it. And I think that's the other piece as well we've learned is making sure we're using tools internally that make us more efficient on those call points, but also using tools and creating tools that we bring into the physician's office like coverage calculators and ways that they can understand who and who does not have coverage, make sure they're efficient and who they prescribe for and how often they prescribe. So the learnings continue, I think we're getting better and better at it. But of course, there's always opportunities to continue to learn.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And our next question comes from the line of Richard Newitter with Truist.

segments.speaker: Ravi Misra
paras: It's actually Ravi here for Rich. Just I want to turn back to the payer comments with CVS. Just trying to understand how you size the risk of potential other payers that you're with going to exclusive peer platforms. And then on Dexcom Direct, can you just walk through the impact that would have on maybe the back end and profitability per patient, DME used to require a little bit more investment -- how does that kind of compare to what they should offer today?

segments.speaker: Jacob Leach
paras: Yes. Thanks for the question, Ravi. As we look at it, most payers -- most of these -- the formularies are, as I mentioned, co-preferred, -- and I think they're like that for a reason. It's about ensuring that their customers, ultimately, they're in the business of serving beneficiaries and -- at this point in time, their beneficiaries want the choice of the systems they use and as do the prescribers and as do the employers. That's why when you look at these employer plans and the custom formularies that many folks operate off of -- they have choice. And I think that's because that's what the customers want.

Now the 2027 formularies are already kind of locked in, so there's no near-term issue there. And as we continue to have conversations throughout the market, we're going to make sure people understand the benefits of our technology as well as our push to ensure that there's equal access for patients that they can get the technology that they need.

segments.speaker: Jereme Sylvain
paras: Yes. And to your question on Dexcom Direct and how that works from an economics perspective, I mean, certainly, we've talked about this other times in the past where there are certain channels that tend to be higher reimbursed DME. There's kind of the middle, which we'll call government. And then there's kind of pharmacy commercial. And all those incur whatever the underlying OpEx burden is associated with it. So you're 100% right there.

As more folks move, for example, from one location to the other, certainly, the costs associated with rightsizing and we've kind of got a pretty good structure to navigate through those right now. So I don't expect there to be a significant underlying cost structure for us because we've already kind of invested in high-volume capabilities across both. There'll be a little bit of a cost of handholding that goes through. So you're absolutely right. There will be a cost underneath it to support the benefits check, the white glove service that we expect to provide for folks. But that would all be embedded in kind of sort of the run rate and investment areas that we make as an organization.

And so in the context, you are right, there's a little bit of an incremental cost associated with it. but we'll ultimately be able to assume that into what I'd say is our growth algorithm because we do make investments. I mean every year, we make investments in the business. And this is one we intended to make irrespective of this announcement. We wanted folks, especially as you had CMS expansion to know what their options were. Because if you remember, CMS expansion is 1 side on the fee-for-service side, but then you've got to navigate to the Medicare Advantage side. And so making sure that we're helping the population navigate, what's a pretty complicated environment. That was always part of the plan, and it'd be part of what of our long-term plans were when we set our LRP out, quite frankly. This is something we've been thinking about for a long, long time.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And our final question comes from the line of Marie Thibault with BTIG.

segments.speaker: Marie Thibault
paras: And I wanted to ask a little bit about operating you've been exceeding expectations on operating and I know you raised the target here for the full year. be thinking about Q4 exiting 2026. I know, obviously, some dynamics with Ireland and shifting spend there. And you've answered the question on not needing to expand the sales force. But what else should we be looking for OpEx and investments needed there, whether that's G8 or other priorities like that?

segments.speaker: Jereme Sylvain
paras: Sure. Yes. I mean I think at least as we think about OpEx for the remainder of this year into next year, you're 100% correct. We are going to make sure we invest in G8. We've got some clinical work to do for G8 as we get ready for submission to the FDA. And so there'll be some investment there. I would expect to see us continue to invest in obviously expansion, and we talked earlier about Dexcom Direct and some investment there. At the same time, remember, we are not investing in an Ireland expansion next year. And so there's an opportunity to gain leverage there. .

So we'll make the right investments in the business to drive growth. But I think you've seen our LRP expectations, and you've seen us historically be able to do it. We can invest in the organization. to invest in the organization. Every year, we add a couple of hundred million dollars OpEx. And so we'll continue to do that, but we can do that while gaining leverage as we're going through the process. And I would expect us to make the investments we need to make but also continue to be able to get the leverage we need to over time in 2027 and quite frankly, beyond. And we laid it out in the LRP, nothing's changed from our thoughts on how we can track towards that.
So thank you for the question, and thank you for the acknowledgment over time. There's been a lot of work and great work by the organization and getting that leverage.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And that concludes our question-and-answer session. I would now like to turn the call back over to Mr. Jake Leach for closing remarks.

segments.speaker: Jacob Leach
paras: Thank you, Abbie. I just want to close the call by saying how proud I am of the execution we delivered this quarter and throughout the year. The progress really reflects the commitment of our employees around the world. And I do want to thank them all for everything they do for Dexcom and for the people we serve. We're confident in our plan. We're energized by the opportunities we see ahead of us, and we're focused on execution. .

And as we head in November, which is National Diabetes Awareness month, it's a meaningful reminder of why the work we do matters and the positive impact we can have on the lives of millions of people living with diabetes. Thank you all for joining us.

segments.speaker: Operator
paras: And ladies and gentlemen, this concludes today's call, and we thank you for your participation. You may now disconnect.
